title: The wheel of the world
hookLine: the seekers describe what they saw: the world as one wheel, spun by nature's three strands around God at the hub
carry: nature turns the wheel; god holds the hub
tomorrow: a swan flies into the wheel
last: ONE LORD BEHIND TIME, FATE AND CHANCE.

lines: ONE RIM, ONE HUB, MANY SPOKES.
cards: Look at a bicycle wheel long enough and it starts to look like an argument. One rim. A hub that barely moves.
Dozens of spokes pulling against each other, and the whole thing works only because the tension is shared. Spin it and the spokes blur. Stop it and you can count them again.
The sages of the Shvetashvatara looked at the world and saw something like that. Not a ladder, not a pyramid. A wheel.
And today's verse does a strange thing with it: it counts the parts.

teach.h: ONE RIM, THREE TIRES, SIXTEEN ENDS.
teach.b: Now the seekers describe what they saw, and verse 1.4 is almost a riddle.
They see the Lord as a wheel with one rim, three tires, sixteen ends, fifty spokes, twenty counter-spokes, six sets of eight, one rope of many forms, three paths, and one delusion with two causes.
Read it once and it's a parts list. Read it with the old commentators and it becomes a map. The one rim is usually read as nature itself, prakriti, the stuff everything is made of.

teach.h: THE OLD MAP: NATURE, POWERS, STATES OF MIND.
teach.b: The sixteen ends are often counted as the five elements plus the eleven powers of body and mind. The fifty spokes, in the commentaries, are fifty states of mind, matching a list known from the school called Samkhya.
Scholars still argue over some of these numbers, and the Upanishad never explains them. Then verse 1.5 turns the wheel into a river with fifty kinds of grief.
But the three tires carry one of Hinduism's most used ideas: the three gunas, the strands of nature.
Sattva, brightness. Rajas, restlessness. Tamas, heaviness.
Food, weather, a mood: all woven from the three. Families still call a meal sattvic, or a slammed-door week all rajas.

teach.h: NATURE TURNS THE WHEEL. GOD HOLDS THE HUB.
teach.b: And here's the teaching: the strands belong to the wheel, to nature. At the hub, the Upanishad says, is the power of God who turns it.
Many teachers draw the lesson the Bhagavad Gita makes plain later: the strands spin, and the self only watches. So a restless week is the wheel turning, not the whole of who you are.

how: Some teachers present the three gunas as a practical way to read one's own moods, and teachers in Vedanta and Samkhya-influenced lineages still explain the world as a turning wheel with the divine at its center.

o: the turning world, all moving around one center
a potter's wheel the gods used to shape clay
a chariot wheel the sages drove into battle

games.q: the wheel and its strands: tap the pairs.

s: the Upanishad explains each number in the wheel itself
it only lists them. the explanations come from later commentators, and scholars still debate some.
the next verse turns the wheel into a river
verse 1.5 pictures five streams, five whirlpools and fifty kinds of grief.
the three tires are usually read as the three gunas
brightness, restlessness and heaviness: the three strands of nature.

games.q: it's been a jumpy, restless week, and you feel like that's just who you are now. what does the wheel of 1.4 suggest?
o: you are your moods; the wheel is you.
that's rajas, a strand of nature spinning. the hub, God, doesn't spin with it.
the wheel is broken and needs to stop.
games.why: the three tires are usually read as the gunas, nature's strands. they turn the wheel; at its center the Upanishad sets the power of God.

practice: Picture a wheel, slowly turning, and notice your own spokes as they pass: a thought, a sound, an itch, a plan. Give each one a strand as it goes by, bright, restless or heavy, without judging it. When you lose track, start again.
For the last few breaths, rest at the center, the part of you that has been watching the strands go by all along.

wordCard.voice: The wheel. The Shvetashvatara's picture of the turning world: one rim, three strands, many spokes, all moving around a center that doesn't move.

orig.note: Sanskrit chakra: wheel. here, the wheel of Brahman that the whole world turns on.

carryVoice: Your line: nature turns the wheel; God holds the hub. Tomorrow, a swan flies into the wheel. See you there.
